quaint-gleanings-from-ancient-poetry-a-c: Antiquarian Edmund Goldsmid gathered odd and charming bits of old verse that had fallen out of fashion. The collection offers curious rhymes, forgotten ballads, and playful poems from centuries past, chosen for their strangeness as much as their beauty. Browsers will find it a cabinet of literary curiosities, full of small surprises from the poetry of earlier ages.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0: The Roman biographer Suetonius profiles Augustus, the first emperor of Rome, in this ancient account written about a century after his death. Readers meet the shrewd young Octavian who ended a hundred years of civil war and rebuilt Rome in marble. Gossipy, vivid, and packed with telling detail, it remains our most colorful source on the man who created the Roman Empire.

Augustus's successor Tiberius was a brilliant general who became a bitter, reclusive emperor. Suetonius recounts his retreat to the island of Capri and the dark rumors that followed him there — stories of cruelty and debauchery that may say as much about Rome's gossip as about the man. A haunting portrait of power curdling into paranoia.

Claudius was the unlikely emperor — mocked for his stammer and limp, yet he conquered Britain and ruled ably for thirteen years. Suetonius gives us a man dominated by his wives, ending with the famous suspicion that Agrippina poisoned him to make way for Nero. History's great underdog emperor, in all his strange contradictions.

Of all Rome's short-lived emperors, Vitellius is remembered as the glutton — a man Suetonius says cared more for feasts than for governing. Seizing power in the chaos of 69 AD, he was dragged through Rome and executed within months. A grotesque, almost comic figure whose biography reads like a warning about appetite unrestrained.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1: Titus earned the title delight of mankind — the emperor who finished the Colosseum and won his people's love. Yet Suetonius reminds us he was also the general who destroyed Jerusalem. Ruling barely two years before his sudden death in 81 AD, he remains one of history's most appealing might-have-beens, glowing all the brighter for his brief reign.
fables-for-the-frivolous: Guy Wetmore Carryl takes Aesop's fables and turns them deliciously upside down in witty verse. The tortoise and the hare, the ants and the grasshopper — all get new, mischievous endings with a modern wink. Clever rhymes and comic illustrations made this 1898 collection a favorite for readers who like their morals served with a laugh.
mediaeval-lore-from-bartholomew-anglicus: In the 1200s, the English friar Bartholomew Anglicus compiled one of the Middle Ages' great encyclopedias, describing everything from angels to ants. These selections gather his most fascinating entries on animals, plants, stones, and the wonders of creation. Reading them is like opening a window onto the medieval mind — curious, devout, and wonderfully strange.
christopher-columbus: Mildred Stapley Byne tells the life of Christopher Columbus — his dreams, his voyages, and his complex legacy — for young readers. The great admiral's story unfolds with the excitement of high adventure. A clear, engaging introduction to the man who changed the world's maps.
thoughts-of-marcus-aurelius: The Meditations of Marcus Aurelius — Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher — gather his private reflections on duty, mortality, and the good life. Written in Greek on military campaigns, these notes to himself have guided readers for eighteen centuries. Timeless wisdom from a ruler who tried to live by philosophy.
toby-tyler-or-ten-weeks-with-a-circus: James Otis' immortal Toby Tyler — ten weeks with a circus — follows the runaway boy through sawdust and spangles to hard-won wisdom. The classic American circus story for children. Every child's favorite since 1881, and still going strong. The skeleton, the fat lady, and kind Mr. Stubbs live in memory.
the-roman-pronunciation-of-latin-why-we-: Frances Lord explains the Roman pronunciation of Latin — why scholars use it and how teachers should teach it — in this clear school manual. Her practical guidance settled many a classroom dispute. A useful little book, still handy for Latin teachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-leub: A 1913 article on Leubus, the great Silesian house on the Oder. Its church is a Baroque wonder. Klemens Löffler records its fortunes. Silesia's pride in stone. Piast dukes chose it for their family tomb. Its abbot ranked as a prince of the Empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbo-cernuus: A 1913 entry on Abbo Cernuus — Abbo the Crooked, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. He sang the siege of Paris by the Northmen in Latin verse. Thomas Walsh gives his life and work. A poet's view of the Viking age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-ortel: A 1913 entry on Abraham Ortelius — the Antwerp mapmaker whose atlas led the world. Joseph Fischer praises the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum. The first modern atlas, born in 1570. The father of map books. His atlas gathered the world's new discoveries. Kings and merchants bought his splendid colored maps.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abundius: A 1913 entry on St. Abundius — the martyr honored in the old calendars. Thomas Walsh notes his scanty record. The Church keeps his name though facts are few. A saint of the early Roman days. His feast falls in the August calendar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abydus: This 1913 reference article on Abydus — the ancient city, in Egypt and on the Hellespont. Leander swam its strait for love. The entry sorts both famous sites. Two old towns, one storied name. Xerxes bridged the strait beside its walls. Its sister city faced it across the strait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accentus-eccl: This 1913 reference article on the accentus ecclesiasticus — the chant tones for prayers and lessons. James Völker explains the musical speech. The liturgy half-sings its words. Plainchant's speaking voice. Deacons still learn its tones in seminary. Its rules fill the old choir books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accessus: This 1913 reference article on accessus — the canon-law approach to a future benefice. John Joseph A'Becket explains the device. Hope of office, secured in advance. Old church law's waiting game. Ambitious clerks watched benefices like hawks. The practice bred simony and was curbed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achaicus: A 1913 entry on Achaicus — the Corinthian Christian who refreshed St. Paul. Anthony Maas notes the single mention. His household served the saints. A small name, honored in Scripture. Paul names him with Fortunatus and Stephanas. Corinth's first fruits, honored forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achiacharus: This 1913 reference piece on Achiacharus — Tobit's nephew, great at the Assyrian court. Wendell Reilly tells his tale from Tobit. He saved his uncle in the dark days. Family loyalty in exile. He rose to cupbearer of the Assyrian king. His fall and rise fill Tobit's tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-actus-primus: A 1913 entry on actus primus — the first act, the form that makes a thing be. Charles Dubray treats the schoolmen's term. Being comes before doing. Metaphysics at its most abstract.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-actus-purus: This 1913 reference piece on actus purus — pure act, without any potency: God Himself. Charles Dubray unfolds the highest name. No becoming, only eternal being. Theology's loftiest definition.
